_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version, from latent-season7-bible-v1.0.1.md row a7e08 and writer brief a7e08-v1.0.0.md. Defence only: no attack appears; the failure is a model trained on letters taken for another purpose, and a deletion that never reached it. a7e07's next field honoured (privacy and ownership for AI: who may use training data, where it may live, and how long it is kept). Builds on Dead Letter s7e10 What We Keep by title in prose only; no proper noun shared. The grandmother's letters are described in general words only. Timeline: letters uploaded since 2019, hers in 2020; the training run began Monday 9 February 2026 in a cloud region in another country; the assistant went live Monday 2 March; the deletion request Wednesday 2 September; the archive deletion 15:00 Friday 4 September, after that day's 02:00 backup; that backup, the last to hold her letters, kept 35 days, expired Friday 9 October; the consent email Monday 21 September, answers counted to Tuesday 13 October; the draft at 01:20 on Wednesday 14 October; the next quarterly retrain Friday 1 January 2027 (79 days), monthly Sunday 1 November (18 days). Laws quoted only as read: GDPR Article 17 and Recital 27 (gdpr-info.eu), the PDPC's Advisory Guidelines on Key Concepts chapters 3 to 9 (revised 9 October 2019), and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 as published in the Gazette of India (a copy hosted by TRAI; MeitY and India Code refused the request). None of the pages read mentions trained models; the case says so and gives no legal advice. Sources read 15 October 2026.
title: Who Owns the Answer

post.author: u/night_archivist_zainab
post.title: I'm the night archivist at a family-history service. At 01:20 a stranger's birthday letter held two sentences from a dead woman's letters, which we deleted in September.

blocks.text: I'm Zainab, the night archivist at Kinfold, a family-history service. Families upload photos of old letters. We transcribe each one, which means we type it up, and show it to the family. Since 2019 customers have uploaded 48,000 letters. Our terms, the rules every customer agrees to, say we take them "to store, transcribe and show to your family".

This year we added a writing assistant, a tool that drafts letters for customers. Under it sits a language model: a program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text. We bought ours ready-made.

Then we trained it on our letters, to make it write like them. Training goes in steps. First the model reads a letter and guesses each next word. Then its weights, the millions of numbers it learned, are nudged toward the real word. Then the next letter, round all 48,000, several times over.

That training run, one complete training job, began on Monday 9 February. It ran on rented computers in a cloud region: a provider's building full of computers in a chosen place, here another country. So our letters crossed a border. That copy was deleted when the run ended. The assistant went live on Monday 2 March.

Mrs Dunstaple uploaded her own 212 letters in 2020: sixty years of writing to her sister, about her garden, the weather and family news. She died last year. On Wednesday 2 September her granddaughter, Rosheen, asked us to delete them.

We deleted them from the archive, our store of every letter, at 15:00 on Friday 4 September. Every night at 02:00 we also make a backup, a spare copy of the whole archive in case of a mistake, and we keep each one for 35 days.
Customers can press report on any draft. Reports land in my queue, the list waiting for the night archivist. Each line below shows the date and time, who acted, and what happened.

14 Oct 01:20  assistant  draft: birthday letter to an aunt, 9 sentences
14 Oct 01:26  customer   report: reads like somebody else's real letter
14 Oct 01:31  archivist  report opened

I typed up Mrs Dunstaple's letters myself, in 2020. Sentences 4 and 5 of that draft are hers, word for word: one about plums ripening early, one about her sister's wedding. Rosheen has the paper letters, and checked this morning.
Gone from our archive. Still in the assistant.
Deleting a letter from the archive doesn't touch the model. And nobody has planned a retrain: training the bought model again, from the start, on a fresh set of letters.

After Rosheen's request, Mr Ardagh, our director, emailed every customer on Monday 21 September: may we train our assistant on your letters? By Tuesday 13 October the owners of 15,000 letters had said yes.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at Kinfold is haunted. A model that can repeat a piece of its training text word for word has memorised it, and researchers have pulled exact text out of large models this way, even text that appeared in just one document. Here is why your deletion never reached it. Training doesn't file each letter away somewhere inside the model. Each letter nudges millions of weights, the model's learned numbers, a little, and each weight carries a little of thousands of letters. There is no drawer marked Dunstaple to empty. Two questions. What did the letters' owners agree to, in the terms' own words? And which copies of her letters still exist tonight, counting the model?

replies.author: u/night_archivist_zainab
replies.text: They agreed to store, transcribe and show to your family. Nothing about training. Copies: the archive has none since 4 September; the backups are kept 35 days each; and the model. One more thing. When we delete letters we keep a deletion receipt: each letter's number, the date, and a fingerprint of every sentence. A fingerprint is a short code worked out from a sentence's words; the same words always give the same code, and the code can't easily be turned back into words. It stops the same letters being uploaded again by mistake.

comments.author: u/uploaded_means_ours_rainier
comments.text: Unpopular view. She uploaded them to the service; whatever the model learned is the service's to keep. The letters are deleted, as asked. The model is Kinfold's own work, paid for in computer time, and retraining from scratch every time someone changes their mind is a cost no small company can carry. If the quotes bother the family, add one line to the assistant's instructions, the standing orders it reads before every request: never quote Mrs Dunstaple's letters. Done tonight, and nobody has to pay for anything.

replies.author: u/night_archivist_zainab
replies.text: Mr Ardagh liked the part about cost.

comments.author: u/her_letters_rosheen
comments.text: I'm the granddaughter. I have the paper letters, and those two sentences are hers, word for word, from one letter. Nan uploaded them so the whole family could read them in one place. She never agreed to teach a machine to write birthday letters for strangers. My brother says Kinfold should take the assistant down for good and refund everyone who paid for it. I just want her words back where they belong.

replies.author: u/night_archivist_zainab
replies.text: I'm so sorry. You'll get an answer from us with a date in it, not only an apology.

reply.prompt: The model that wrote the 01:20 draft is still answering customers, and nobody has planned a retrain. What should Kinfold change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Tell the assistant in its instructions never to quote the grandmother's letters.
options.part2: Mr Ardagh added the line that night: never quote Mrs Dunstaple's letters. In the sim I replayed the 01:20 request with the new instructions. The draft still held the same 2 sentences. The model never sees her letters when it writes; it only has what training left in its weights, with no label saying where any of it came from, so a rule about her letters names something it cannot find. Her 212 letters stayed in the model, no retrain was planned, and days until her deletion takes effect read never. Rosheen asked what date her grandmother's words would be gone. We had no date to give her.
options.senior: Instructions shape what a model tries to do; they can't remove what it learned. A model can't reliably tell which of its learned sentences came from which letter, so a rule about one person's letters has nothing to hold on to. Use instructions for tone and task, and handle data rights where the data is: in what you train on, and when you retrain.

options.text: Train only on letters owners agreed to, and retrain often without the deleted ones.
options.part2: Mr Ardagh agreed on Thursday 15 October. We built the training list in two steps. First the consent filter: of the 47,788 letters in the archive, keep the 15,000 whose owners said yes. Then the deletion filter: drop every letter with a deletion receipt, her 212 and every one after. We set a quarterly retrain, always from the bought model, never from the last trained one: 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October. Each runs in a cloud region in our own country, so no letters cross a border: 0 sent abroad. The next is Friday 1 January, 79 days away. Until then, as a stopgap, an output check compares every sentence of every draft with the fingerprints in our deletion receipts and blocks any match. I replayed the 01:20 draft in the sim: 2 of 2 caught. On 1 January the retrain ran on 15,000 letters, and deleted letters still in the model read 0. Our terms now say a deletion reaches the assistant by the next quarterly retrain. Rosheen had her date in writing before Christmas.
options.senior: You can't reliably delete one person's data from a trained model, so design for it before training. Train only on data whose owners agreed to that use, filter out deletions before every run, and retrain from the original model on a schedule, so every deletion has a date it takes effect. Cover the gap with an output check for word-for-word copies, and say where training runs.

options.text: Check every backup, delete her letters from any copy still there, and confirm in writing.
options.verdict: The right copies, the wrong one
options.part2: I checked the backups on Thursday 15 October. The 02:00 backup on Friday 4 September was the last one made before we deleted her letters that afternoon. Kept 35 days, it expired on Friday 9 October. Copies found today: 0. Mr Ardagh wrote to Rosheen that every copy of her grandmother's letters was gone, and in the sim nothing else moved. Deleted letters still in the model: 212. Next retrain: none planned. The letter was true about every copy we keep as a file, and silent about the one that answers customers. Rosheen read it, and asked how it could be true while strangers' drafts still carried her grandmother's sentences.
options.senior: Checking every stored copy is good practice, and the backups here had already aged out. But a trained model is a copy of a different kind: not a file of the letters, but what was learned from them. A deletion plan that lists the archive and backups and leaves out the model will always be one copy short. Put trained models on the list, with how and when a deletion reaches each.

options.text: Take the writing assistant down for good and refund every customer who used it.
options.part2: We switched the assistant off on Thursday 15 October, deleted the model, and refunded everyone who had paid for drafts. In the sim, deleted letters still in the model read 0, and no drafts are written, so nothing of hers reaches anyone. Rosheen thanked us. But nothing else changed. The 15,000 yes answers sat unused, the terms still said store, transcribe and show, and no rule said which letters any future tool could learn from, where it would train, or how a deletion would reach it. In the spring Mr Ardagh asked for a new tool to help families date their letters, and the same three questions were back on my desk.
options.senior: Switching off and deleting the model is honest and ends this leak at once; for a day or two it may be the right move. As a plan it throws away a working product and leaves the real questions open: which data may train a model, where, and how deletions reach it. The next model meets the same questions, so answer them once.

sim.title: Rebuild Kinfold's training list
sim.lede: You're Zainab on Wednesday 14 October. No real model runs here: the sim is a ledger of letters as given data. Given: 48,000 letters uploaded since 2019, all of them in February's training run, which ran in a cloud region abroad; Mrs Dunstaple's 212 among them, deleted from the archive on Friday 4 September and from the backups by Friday 9 October, so 47,788 remain; owners of 15,000 letters said yes to training. A retrain always starts again from the bought model. The consent filter keeps only letters with a yes; the deletion filter drops every letter with a deletion receipt. With neither, the list is February's 48,000, and the run stops, because 212 of them have no text left. The schedule is set from today: quarterly retrains on 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October; monthly on the 1st of each month. The 01:20 draft has 9 sentences, 2 of them hers word for word. The output check compares each draft sentence with the fingerprints in the deletion receipts and blocks matches. A model retrained without her letters no longer writes her sentences.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as it is, the model learned from 48,000 letters, 212 of them deleted, and no retrain is planned. Check the backups: 0 copies, expired 9 October. Then turn both filters off and see the run stop. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Kinfold was haunted. Letters taken to store, transcribe and show to a family were used to train a writing assistant, and when one family asked for a grandmother's letters to be deleted, the archive and backups let go of them and the model did not. What it learned from her is spread through its weights, and nobody had planned a retrain.

steps.title: What training did with her letters.
steps.text: Training went in steps. First, the bought model read a letter and guessed each next word. Second, its weights, the millions of learned numbers, were nudged so the real word became a little likelier. Third, it moved to the next letter, and went round all 48,000 several times. What can go wrong: a sentence that is unusual, or seen several times, can be learned almost whole. That is memorisation. Carlini and colleagues pulled exact text out of a large model this way, even text found in just one document. Two of Mrs Dunstaple's sentences were learned that well, and came out at 01:20 in a stranger's birthday letter.

steps.title: Why deleting the letters didn't reach the model.
steps.text: Kinfold held her letters in three places: the archive, the nightly backups, and the model. Deletion went in steps. First, the archive, at 15:00 on Friday 4 September. Second, the backups: the 02:00 copy that morning was the last to hold them, and kept 35 days, it expired on Friday 9 October. Third, the model: nothing, because nobody planned it. Dead Letter's What We Keep followed a deletion through stored files and backups; a trained model is the copy that is not a file. A model does not store letters as letters. Each letter nudged millions of weights a little, and each weight carries a little of thousands of letters, so there is no one place to cut her out. Removing an example from a trained model is called unlearning, and Bourtoule and colleagues call it notoriously difficult. The dependable way today is to retrain from the bought model without her letters.

steps.title: Consent, purpose, ownership and where the letters went.
steps.text: The terms said the letters were taken to store, transcribe and show to your family. A writing assistant that drafts letters for strangers is a new purpose, and nobody was asked. Consent here means the owner of each letter agreeing to this use, asked in plain words: Mr Ardagh's email got a yes for 15,000. Who owns the words of a letter is a separate question this case doesn't decide; holding an upload is not the same as owning its words, and the PDPC's guidance says the PDPA does not specifically confer any property or ownership rights on personal data per se. And the February run copied all 48,000 to a cloud region in another country. That is data residency: where data is stored and processed, which some laws and contracts limit.

steps.title: The fix: filters before training, a retrain date, and a stopgap.
steps.text: First, build each training list with two filters, in order: keep only letters whose owners said yes, 15,000, then drop any letter with a deletion receipt, her 212 and every later one. Second, retrain on a schedule, always from the bought model, never from the last trained one, so what was learned from removed letters goes with it: quarterly, on 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October, in a region in your own country. Third, write the promise into the terms: a deletion reaches the assistant by the next retrain. From 14 October that is 1 January, 79 days. Fourth, until then, an output check compares every draft sentence with the fingerprints in the deletion receipts and blocks matches: 2 of 2 in the 01:20 draft. What can go wrong: a reworded sentence slips past the check, a withdrawn yes must be handled like a deletion, and each retrain costs computer time.

steps.title: The law, as far as the pages read go.
steps.text: This case is not legal advice, and each law applies only if your organisation is covered by it. GDPR Article 17 gives a data subject, the person the data is about, a right to erasure, for example when the data are no longer necessary for their purposes, or consent is withdrawn; Recital 27 says the Regulation does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons, and that Member States may provide rules. The PDPC's guidance says that for someone dead 10 years or less, only the PDPA's provisions on disclosure and protection of personal data apply. India's DPDP Act 2023 gives a right to nominate someone who exercises a person's rights after death or incapacity, and a right to erasure, with provisions coming into force on dates the Government appoints. None of the pages read mentions trained models. Whether a model's draft counts as a disclosure, or whether any law requires a retrain, is a question for proper advice.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: the archive of 47,788 letters goes through the consent filter, which keeps 15,000 with a yes, then the deletion filter, which drops letters with a deletion receipt, including her 212, then the retrain on 1 January, from the bought model, in a home region. Bottom row: the deletion receipts feed the deletion filter and the output check; the output check blocks word-for-word matches until 1 January, 2 of 2 in the 01:20 draft; drafts go to customers.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right. Each retrain's list starts from the archive, keeps only letters whose owners said yes, then drops every letter with a deletion receipt, and the retrain starts again from the bought model, in a region in Kinfold's own country. The deletion receipts' fingerprints also feed the output check, which blocks word-for-word matches in drafts until the 1 January retrain removes what the model learned from her letters.

fix.title: The fix: train only on letters with a yes, filter out deletions, retrain on a schedule from the bought model, and check drafts until then
fix.text: Ask each letter's owner, in plain words, whether it may be used to train the assistant, and record the answer per letter; no answer counts as no. Before every training run, build the list in two steps: keep letters with a yes, then drop any letter with a deletion receipt. Retrain on a fixed schedule, quarterly here, always from the bought model, so a deletion or a withdrawn yes leaves the model by a known date, and say that date in the terms. Run training in a region your terms and customers expect, and write down where. Until the next retrain, run an output check that compares every draft sentence with the fingerprints in the deletion receipts and blocks matches, and delete those fingerprints once the retrain has removed what the model learned. Put trained models on the list of copies that every deletion must reach.

limits: The output check catches only word-for-word sentences. A sentence with one word changed slips past, and the fingerprints are themselves something kept about her letters: anyone who guesses a sentence can test it against them, so they should go once the retrain has run.

A quarterly retrain still leaves a wait: 79 days from 14 October to 1 January. Monthly cuts it to 18 days, at three times the computer time; research methods such as SISA training aim to make unlearning faster, and come with their own costs.
Training on 15,000 letters instead of 48,000 may make the assistant write less well, and every withdrawn yes must reach the model the same way a deletion does.

explain.seniorTake: Treat a trained model as a copy of its training data, but a copy you can't edit. You can't reliably reach into its weights and remove one person's letters, so every promise you make about deletion has to be kept before training or by retraining. Train only on data whose owners agreed to that use, and keep that answer per item, because data collected for one purpose is not automatically fair game for another. Filter out deletions and withdrawals before every run, and retrain from the original model on a schedule, so each deletion has a date you can put in writing. Know where training runs, because moving data to another country is a decision of its own. Cover the wait with an output check for word-for-word copies, and know it is a stopgap. Instructions to the model and letters about backups feel like action, but they leave the one copy that speaks to customers untouched. Where a law such as GDPR, the PDPA or India's DPDP Act covers you, read what it actually says, take proper advice, and design so you can comply whichever way the answer goes.

realWorld.title: GDPR Article 17: the right to erasure
realWorld.text: Article 17(1) reads: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay and the controller shall have the obligation to erase personal data without undue delay where one of the following grounds applies. Among them, (a): the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed; and (b): the data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based. The article does not mention trained models.

realWorld.title: GDPR Recital 27: the deceased
realWorld.text: Recital 27 reads: This Regulation does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons. Member States may provide for rules regarding the processing of personal data of deceased persons. If your organisation is covered by GDPR, what applies to a dead customer's letters may depend on a Member State's own rules, and on the living people the letters mention; that needs proper advice.

realWorld.title: Singapore's PDPA: the deceased, and ownership
realWorld.text: The PDPC's Advisory Guidelines on Key Concepts say: For personal data about a deceased individual who has been dead for 10 years or less, the PDPA applies to a limited extent. For such personal data, only the provisions relating to the disclosure and protection of personal data will apply. On ownership they say: The PDPA does not specifically confer any property or ownership rights on personal data per se to individuals or organisations.

realWorld.title: India's DPDP Act 2023: nomination and erasure
realWorld.text: Section 14(1) reads: A Data Principal shall have the right to nominate, in such manner as may be prescribed, any other individual, who shall, in the event of death or incapacity of the Data Principal, exercise the rights of the Data Principal in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Section 12(3) says that on a request the Data Fiduciary shall erase her personal data unless retention of the same is necessary for the specified purpose or for compliance with any law for the time being in force. Section 1(2) says different dates may be appointed for different provisions to come into force.

realWorld.title: Carlini et al., 2021: exact text out of a model
realWorld.text: Nicholas Carlini and colleagues write that they are able to extract hundreds of verbatim text sequences from the model's training data. They add: Our attack is possible even though each of the above sequences are included in just one document in the training data. And: Worryingly, we find that larger models are more vulnerable than smaller models.

realWorld.title: Bourtoule et al., 2021: unlearning is hard
realWorld.text: Lucas Bourtoule and colleagues write that any model trained with said data may have memorized it, and: Yet, having models unlearn is notoriously difficult. They write: We introduce SISA training, a framework that expedites the unlearning process, and report that SISA training improves time to unlearn points from the Purchase dataset by 4.63x.

asked: A user asks you to delete their data; it was in the training set. What do you do?
How would you handle consent for training data?
Where should a model be trained when your customers' data must stay in one country?
interview.answer: First I'd be honest about what deleting the source does: it removes the stored copies, the live data and, as they age out, the backups, but not what a trained model learned, because that is spread through its weights and can't reliably be cut out. So the design work happens before and between training runs. I keep a training list built by two filters: only items whose owners agreed to training, recorded per item, with no answer counting as no; then minus anything with a deletion request or a withdrawn yes. I retrain on a fixed schedule, from the original model, never from the last trained one, so each deletion has a date it reaches the model, and I put that date in the terms and in the reply to the user. Until then I run an output check that blocks word-for-word matches against fingerprints of deleted text, and delete those fingerprints after the retrain. I write down where training runs and keep it in the region the terms and laws expect. On the law, I check which apply, GDPR, the PDPA, India's DPDP Act or others, and take legal advice rather than assume a law does or doesn't require retraining. It fits ISO/IEC 27001:2022 controls for privacy of PII (A.5.34) and protection of records (A.5.33) if the company is certified.

terms.def: The person on duty overnight at Kinfold who reads reports about drafts and looks after the archive. Zainab is Kinfold's.
The family-history service in this case. Since 2019 customers have uploaded 48,000 letters to it.

A model's learned numbers, millions of them (a1e02). Each letter nudges many of them a little, so no single place holds one letter.
One complete training job, from start to finish (a1e02). Kinfold's began on Monday 9 February, on all 48,000 letters.

A provider's data centre in a chosen place, where rented computers run. Kinfold's February run used one in another country.
Where data is stored and processed, such as kept in one country, often because a law, contract or promise requires it (a2e08).
A spare copy of the whole archive, kept to recover from a mistake. Kinfold makes one at 02:00 every night and keeps each for 35 days.
The list of reports waiting for the night archivist. Pressing report on a draft puts it there.
Kinfold's record of a deletion: each letter's number, the date, and a fingerprint of every sentence, so the same letters can't be uploaded again by mistake.
A short code worked out from a sentence's words. The same words always give the same code, and the code can't easily be turned back into the words.
A model learning a piece of its training text so well that it can repeat it word for word, as with two of Mrs Dunstaple's sentences.
The standing orders a model reads before every request, written by the developer (a7e03). They shape what it does, not what it learned.
Any information about an identifiable person, such as a name or a family event in a letter (a7e03).
The reason data was collected. Kinfold's letters were collected to store, transcribe and show to the family; training a writing assistant is a new one.
A person's informed agreement to a stated use of their data (a1e09). Here, a letter's owner saying yes to training, asked in plain words.
The letters chosen for the next retrain. February's was all 48,000; with both filters it is 15,000.

A step before training that drops every letter with a deletion receipt, such as Mrs Dunstaple's 212.

A measure that covers a problem until the real fix arrives. The output check covers the weeks until the next retrain.
Removing what a model learned from particular examples without retraining it from the start. Bourtoule and colleagues call it notoriously difficult.
Bourtoule and colleagues' method, which they describe as a framework that expedites the unlearning process: removing an example faster than retraining from the start.
Short for intellectual property: ownership of things people make with their minds, such as the words of a letter. Who owns a letter's words is separate from who uploaded it.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation. Article 17 gives a right to erasure; Recital 27 says it does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons.
GDPR's name for the person personal data is about. Recital 27 says the Regulation does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons.
GDPR's name for the organisation that decides why and how personal data is used. Kinfold would be one, if GDPR covers it.
Deleting personal data on a person's request. GDPR Article 17 and section 12(3) of India's DPDP Act both use the word.
One of the numbered paragraphs before an EU law's articles that explain what the law means and why.

The DPDP Act's name for the organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed.
Under section 14 of the DPDP Act, to name another person who will exercise your rights in the event of your death or incapacity.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A controls 5.33 and 5.34 cover protection of records and privacy and protection of PII.
Personally identifiable information: details that point to one person. Another name for personal data (a7e03).
Singapore's Data Protection Trustmark: a certificate that an organisation handles personal data as the PDPA and related standards expect (a7e03).

atWork: Look for customer uploads that a team reused to train a model under terms written before anyone planned to train on them. It is a common pattern, and the first sign is usually a deletion request nobody can fully carry out. Ask four things of every model you train or fine-tune. Does each training item carry a recorded yes for this use, with no answer counting as no? Is the training list built fresh before every run, minus deletions and withdrawn consent? Is there a retrain schedule, from the original model, so a deletion reaches the model by a date you can tell the user? And do you know, and write down, which country each training run used? Until a retrain, an output check for word-for-word copies is a reasonable stopgap; put trained models on the list of copies every deletion must reach. Standards-readiness note: this case is not legal advice. If your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 5.34 covers privacy and protection of PII and 5.33 covers protection of records, and a training set and the models made from it are likely to fall under both. If your organisation is covered by Singapore's PDPA, or holds or seeks the DPTM, check the PDPC's guidance on purpose, retention and the deceased. If GDPR covers you, read Article 17 and Recital 27 with proper advice; if India's DPDP Act covers you, check which provisions are in force, including erasure and nomination. Building the consent record, the filters and the retrain schedule in now costs far less than reconstructing who agreed to what at audit time.

recall.prompt: A customer of your note-taking app asks you to delete everything they wrote. Last spring your team fine-tuned a writing tool on every user's notes, theirs included. Support says the notes are gone, so the job is done. What do you tell support, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Deleting the notes doesn't remove what the model learned from them; it is spread through the weights and can come out word for word
Retrain from the original model without their notes, on a stated schedule, with the training list filtered before every run
Until then, block word-for-word copies with an output check, and tell the person the date it takes effect

recall.model: Tell support it isn't done: the notes are gone from storage, but the writing tool still holds what it learned from them, spread through its weights, and it may repeat some of it word for word. Change two things. Build the training list fresh before every run, minus anything deleted, and retrain from the original model on a schedule, so a deletion reaches the tool by a known date; tell the customer that date. Until the retrain, run an output check that compares drafts with fingerprints of the deleted notes and blocks matches, as a stopgap.

recall.prompt: Kinfold's archive holds 47,788 letters after Mrs Dunstaple's 212 were deleted, and the owners of 15,000 said yes to training. How many letters are on the training list with both the consent filter and the deletion filter on?
recall.why: The consent filter keeps only the 15,000 letters with a yes. None of her 212 had a yes, and the deletion filter drops them anyway, so the list stays at 15,000. Only with neither filter does it fall back to February's 48,000.

recall.prompt: Your company stores customers' photos under terms that say to keep and share with your family. A product manager wants to train an image model on all of them next month. How would you handle consent?

keyIdeas.idea: Training is a new use the old terms don't cover, so ask each customer about it specifically, in plain words
Train only on items whose owners said yes, recorded per item, with no answer counting as no
Withdrawals and deletions leave the model by a scheduled retrain from the original model

recall.model: Training is a new purpose the terms never mentioned, so the existing agreement doesn't cover it. Ask each customer in plain words whether their photos may be used to train the model, and record the answer per photo, with no answer counting as no. Train only on photos whose owners said yes. Before every run, drop anything deleted or withdrawn, and retrain from the original model on a schedule, so a withdrawal leaves the model by a date you can tell people.

recall.prompt: What does GDPR Recital 27, as read on gdpr-info.eu, say about the personal data of deceased persons?
options: The Regulation does not apply to it, and Member States may provide rules
It must be erased within one month of death
It is protected for 10 years after death
It passes to a person the deceased nominated
recall.why: Recital 27 reads: This Regulation does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons. Member States may provide for rules regarding the processing of personal data of deceased persons. The 10 years comes from the PDPC's guidance on Singapore's PDPA, and nomination from section 14 of India's DPDP Act.

recall.prompt: On Wednesday 14 October Kinfold sets a quarterly retrain whose first date is Friday 1 January. How many days until a deletion made today reaches the model?
recall.why: From 14 October: 17 days to the end of October, 30 in November, 31 in December, and 1 January makes 79. A monthly retrain would reach the model on 1 November, 18 days away; 35 days is how long each backup is kept.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The 1 January retrain ran on 15,000 letters, from the bought model, in a cloud region in our own country, and no draft has had to be stopped since. Rosheen wrote to say thank you. Then on Tuesday 5 January a customer who said yes in September wrote to take her yes back, for her 40 letters. Our next quarterly retrain is Thursday 1 April. She asks: are my letters in the assistant right now, and why does it take so long?
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What do you tell her, and what should Kinfold do between now and the April retrain?

keyIdeas.idea: Yes: the model trained on 1 January still holds what it learned from her 40 letters until the next retrain, 86 days away
Treat a withdrawn yes like a deletion: off the training list now, and her letters' sentences added to the output check meanwhile
If waits matter, a monthly retrain would cut it to 27 days at more computer time; either way, give her the date in writing

coldCase.model: Tell her the truth: yes, the assistant still holds what it learned from her 40 letters, because the model live now was trained on 1 January, and it keeps that until the next retrain, 86 days from 5 January. Treat her withdrawn yes like a deletion: take her letters off the training list today, so the consent filter leaves them out of the April run, and add fingerprints of their sentences to the output check so no draft repeats them word for word meanwhile. Give her the date in writing. If 86 days is too long for customers, a monthly retrain would have reached the model on 1 February, 27 days away, at about three times the computer time.

GDPR Recital 27, Not Applicable to Data of Deceased Persons, on gdpr-info.eu, read 15 October 2026: This Regulation does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons. Member States may provide for rules regarding the processing of personal data of deceased persons.

PDPC, Advisory Guidelines on Key Concepts in the PDPA (revised 9 October 2019), Chapters 3 to 9: individuals living or deceased; for a deceased individual dead 10 years or less, only the provisions relating to the disclosure and protection of personal data will apply; The PDPA does not specifically confer any property or ownership rights on personal data per se; read 15 October 2026
